claim: In an LLM post-training pipeline, a clean (unpoisoned) preference optimization stage (DPO or PPO) following a poisoned supervised fine-tuning stage can reduce the attack success rate of the SFT-embedded backdoor to near zero, masking its presence.
falsifier: Reproduce the experiment with a different model family and a different preference optimization algorithm (e.g., KTO) to test whether the suppression effect holds.

conditions: SFT stage is poisoned with a backdoor
preference optimization stage is clean (no poisoning)
preference optimization uses standard DPO or PPO
exclusions: Evidence is limited to the reported model, dataset, trigger, and experimental conditions; transfer to other models, tasks, or pipelines is unestablished.

title: Presence of a clean–attack success rate mechanism
